title: What I did yesterday
title_target: 어제 뭐 했어요 — Eoje mwo haesseoyo
goal: Talk about things that have already happened using the past tense, and see how Korean marks time inside the verb itself — not only with time words.
bekal: form the past tense -았어요/었어요 from a verb stem
make the past tense of 이에요 and 있어요
negate past events with 안 and 못
describe your weekend in a few sentences in a row
use 그리고, 그래서 and 하지만 to link a story together

dialogs.title: 대화 — Monday morning in class
dialogs.intro: Suji asks about Ani's weekend. Notice that no word like "already" or "ago" is needed — Korean puts that time information inside the verb.

lines.speaker: 수지:
lines.id: Ani, what did you do on the weekend?

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: On Saturday I met a friend. We went to Myeongdong together.
lines.literal: Saturday-on — friend — object — met. together — Myeongdong-to — went.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: A few clothes. Then we ate tteokbokki.
lines.literal: clothes — object — a-little — bought. and — tteokbokki — object — ate.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: It was delicious! But a bit spicy.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: I didn't do anything. I rested at home.

lines.speaker: 아니:
lines.id: Oh… I couldn't. I didn't have time.
lines.literal: ah… couldn't — did. time — subject — didn't-exist.

notes: **The Korean past tense attaches to the verb rather than standing as a separate word.** English sometimes adds "did", "have" or "already"; Korean simply changes the verb itself. 먹어요 (eat) → 먹**었**어요 (ate). Time words are optional — the verb form is not.

**The past is built from the 해요 form you already know**, so there's no new rule to memorize. Remove 요 from the 해요 form and add ㅆ어요. 가요 → 가**ㅆ**어요 → 갔어요. 먹어요 → 먹었어요. 마셔요 → 마셨어요. Once you see the pattern, it works for every verb, no exceptions.

**안 and 못 both negate, but for different reasons.** 안 했어요 = didn't do it (chose not to, didn't intend to). 못 했어요 = couldn't, didn't get to (something got in the way). When Ani says 못 했어요 about her homework, she's saying "it's not that I was lazy" — and the difference is felt.
**아무것도 always pairs with a negative.** 아무것도 **안** 했어요 = didn't do anything. ⚠️ 아무것도 했어요 isn't a sentence. Think of English "not … anything"; the same goes for 아무도 (anyone) and 아무 데도 (anywhere).

**Adjectives take the past tense too, exactly like verbs.** 맛있어요 → 맛있**었**어요, 매워요 → 매**웠**어요. In Korean, adjectives behave like verbs: they can be put in the past, negated, and stand alone as the predicate with no "to be".

**매워요 comes from 맵다, not 매우다.** It's an irregular ㅂ verb: ㅂ turns into 우 before a vowel. 맵다 → 매워요 → 매웠어요. This group includes many key adjectives: 덥다 (hot) → 더워요, 춥다 (cold) → 추워요, 쉽다 (easy) → 쉬워요, 어렵다 (difficult) → 어려워요.

**너무 used to mean "too" and now more often means "very".** 너무 맛있어요 doesn't mean "too tasty" but "really delicious". For compliments this is completely natural. If you really mean "too", it shows in a complaining tone or a pattern like 너무 … 아서 + the problem.
**떡볶이 is read *tteokbokki*, not *tteokbokgi*.** It's the tensing rule after a stopped sound, explained in the front pages. You'll see this word often, and beginners often misread it.

grammars.title: The past tense -았어요 / -었어요
body: The rule is exactly the same as the 해요 form you've already mastered — only the ending differs. Look at the last vowel in the stem.
after: **A shortcut that always works:** take the 해요 form, drop 요, attach ㅆ어요. 봐요 → 봐 + ㅆ어요 → 봤어요. Not a single verb breaks this shortcut.
**The past of "to be" and "to exist":** 이에요 → **이었어요**, 예요 → **였어요**, 있어요 → **있었어요**, 없어요 → **없었어요**. Learn these four as they are.
⚠️ Korean has no separate "have done" or "just did" forms like English. This one past form covers them all, and the nuance comes from adverbs: 아까 (earlier), 벌써 (already), 방금 (just now).

grammars.title: 안 and 못 — two ways to say no
body: Both go **directly in front of the verb**, and both work the same in the present and the past.
after: ⚠️ **하다 verbs split in the middle.** It's 공부 안 해요, not 안 공부해요. The noun stands on its own, 안 goes in between, then 해요. This applies to every 하다 verb: 일 안 해요, 운동 안 해요, 요리 안 해요.
**못 is more polite for turning down an invitation.** 안 가요 sounds like "I just don't want to"; 못 가요 sounds like "sorry, I can't make it". To decline an invitation, 못 is almost always the one.
There's a third, gentler and more written negative: **-지 않다**. 가지 않아요 = 안 가요. It comes back in unit 12.

sections.title: Telling the story of a day gone by

blocks.text: Storytelling doesn't come from long sentences, but from several short sentences linked correctly. These connectors are enough for all of A1.
토요일에 친구를 만났어요. 같이 명동에 갔어요. 거기에서 옷을 샀어요. 그리고 떡볶이를 먹었어요. 너무 맛있었어요. 하지만 조금 매웠어요. 일요일에는 아무것도 안 했어요. 집에서 쉬었어요. 그래서 지금 괜찮아요.
Nine sentences, all short, all using material you already have. This is the kind of story expected at TOPIK level 1 — not layered sentences, but simple sentences that are correct and connected.

blocks.title: The most useful practice in this whole unit
items: Every night before bed, tell your day in five Korean sentences. Out loud, not in your head.
Don't hunt for words you don't have yet. Tell only what you can with what you have — that's exactly what builds flexibility.
If there's one word you truly need every day, that's the word worth looking up. Vocabulary that comes from your own needs sticks far better than a memorized list.

exercises.prompt: Fill in 안 or 못 according to the hint.
items: I simply don't want to go: 저는 ____ 가요.
I didn't get to do my homework: 숙제를 ____ 했어요.
I don't eat meat: 고기를 ____ 먹어요.
I couldn't come because I was sick: ____ 왔어요.
I didn't study today: 오늘 공부 ____ 했어요.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Korean using the past tense.
items: What did you do on the weekend?

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: 먹었어요 — 갔어요 — 봤어요 — 공부했어요 — 마셨어요 — 있었어요
